#+title: Special member functions and RAII
#+summary: Even an empty C++ class has a default constructor, a copy constructor, a copy assignment and a destructor generated by the compiler (plus move operations since C++11); they copy and destroy member by member, and ~= default~ / ~= delete~ request or forbid them explicitly.

* Definition
For =class A {};= the compiler provides
#+begin_src c++
  A a;              // A::A()                    default constructor
  A a2(a);          // A::A(const A&)            copy constructor
  a = a2;           // A& A::operator=(const A&) copy assignment
  A* pa = new A();  delete pa;   // A::~A()      destructor
#+end_src
and, from C++11, =A(A&&)= and =A& operator=(A&&)= (see [[id:move-semantics][move semantics]]). The generated versions work member by member: copy each member, destroy each member.
- Declaring any constructor with parameters removes the implicit default constructor: =A a;= stops compiling unless =A() = default;= is added back.
- ~= delete~ forbids an operation: =A(const A&) = delete;= makes =A= non-copyable.
- The [[id:shallow-deep-copy][copy constructor]] is called for initialisation (=A b(a)=, =A b = a=, pass and return by value); ~operator=~ for assignment to an existing object.

* RAII
Resource Acquisition Is Initialisation: the constructor acquires a resource (memory, file, lock), the destructor releases it. Since destructors run automatically when an object goes out of scope, also during exception unwinding, the resource can never leak. =std::string=, =std::vector=, =std::unique_ptr=, =std::lock_guard= are all RAII classes.

* Worked example
#+begin_src c++
  A f(A x) { return x; }   // which special members run?

  int main() {
    A a;          // A(): default constructor
    A b = a;      // A(const A&): copy constructor (initialisation, not assignment)
    b = a;        // operator=(const A&): copy assignment
    A c = f(a);   // A(const A&) builds the parameter x;
                  // A(A&&) builds the result (a returned parameter is moved);
                  // ~A() destroys x at the end of the statement
  }               // ~A() for c, b, a: reverse order of construction
#+end_src

* Intuition
The compiler writes the boring members for you, and they are right as long as every member manages itself. The moment a member is a raw owning pointer, they are wrong.

* Pitfall
~operator=~ returns =A&= (=*this=) so that =a = b = c= works as =a = (b = c)=, and must survive self-assignment =a = a=.
